slides.title: The AI Proposes, A Verified Human Decides
slides.subtitle: CoreOps  ·  a Colaberry learner build
slides.caption: Operations teams do not distrust automation because it is inaccurate. They distrust it because they cannot see what it did.

slides.title: The problem is governance, not modelling.
slides.subtitle: A model can already read telemetry and suggest a fix.
slides.caption: What it cannot do is establish that a person agreed, that they were who they claimed to be, and that the agreement can be shown to someone else weeks later.
Telemetry in, a proposal out, and a boundary in the middle that the system cannot cross on its own.
The guardrails tab states what is enforced and what is not, rather than implying everything is.

slides.title: The model proposes. It cannot apply.
slides.subtitle: The boundary is enforced in code, not written in a policy document.
slides.caption: A policy evaluator decides whether an action is permissible at all, and anything that would write is held in a queue until a person acts.

rows: guardrail modules, 4 with their own tests
slides.caption: A system whose central claim is that its choices are provable after the fact has written its choices down.
Every requirement traced to the thing that satisfies it, in the system's own command centre.

slides.title: Approval survives the session that made it.
slides.subtitle: Identity is part of the boundary, not a login problem.
slides.caption: One decision record commits to multi-factor authentication on the approving account; another binds approval to a verified identity rather than to a session.

slides.title: 46 of 292 files carry a test.
slides.subtitle: And whether the remediations are correct was not measured.
slides.caption: Both are published on the record rather than left out. The system proves who agreed to a change, not that the change was the right one.
